messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At seventy-one, Arthur’s life was still anchored to the locked bedroom of his childhood, where his mother’s partner used his larger frame to enforce a cruel, unpredictable order. The abuser’s heavy boots and the sharp, sweet-stale smell of alcohol became the anchors of that terror. When Arthur finally revisited those years, he described how the sudden pieces of the event would materialize in his mind without warning, only to vanish as quickly as they arrived. Those fragments felt more real than the ordinary days he was trying to live, and their visceral immediacy directly sharpened his threat perception, turning ordinary quiet into a tense waiting game. The vivid, more-real-than-normal memories of that locked room meant that the sharp whiff of that old alcohol or the wail of a passing siren instantly primed his nervous system to scan for that same sensory signature years later. Because the man who hurt him had been trusted to provide safety, Arthur had come to believe he had been betrayed by someone he trusted, with the fact that the people responsible had faced no consequences hardening his conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe. The sheer weight of these memories directly drove him to construct mental barriers, prompting him to keep his mind occupied all the time and to strictly avoid television programmes or films that echoed his childhood trauma. The specific sensory anchors of that era now governed his daily existence. When a colleague’s voice grew slightly sharp during a routine insurance claims review inside his downtown cubicle, or when a delivery driver’s car idled too long at the curb outside the building, Arthur felt threatened by strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations. These encounters with strangers instantly reinforced his negative appraisal that ordinary conversations were thinly veiled threats, which in turn sharpened his threat perception into a constant state of hyper-vigilance. Believing the world was inherently hostile made him hyper-aware of triggers he once would have ignored; the wail of a siren now commanded his immediate attention, just as it had decades ago. He would listen for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home, treating every settling floorboard as a potential intrusion, and his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. When he would wake up startled, convinced someone was in the room, his body’s frantic response only reinforced his appraisal that his own nervous system had become an enemy he couldn’t control. Feeling threatened by strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations, meant that every knock at the door or unfamiliar car window rolling down became a new activation point, while his mind constantly scavenged earlier fragments to validate the current alarm. The exhausting cycle of false alarms and perceived hostility directly pushed him to perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, ensuring his mind never settled. Performing mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, while simultaneously keeping his mind occupied all the time to block out the past, only taught him that he was fundamentally incapable of staying safe without constant effort, deepening his sense of vulnerability. Avoiding TV programmes or films that echoed his childhood trauma left no alternative frameworks for safety, which directly pushed his threat perception to scan his insurance office cubicle and his suburban driveway for familiar cues of danger. This relentless internal management only amplified his threat perception, turning a neighbor’s casual wave into a potential intrusion that demanded a calculated, cautious response. Over the decades, his insurance office became the primary stage for his avoidance behaviours; he began routing all client paperwork through digital portals to prevent face-to-face interactions, and he strictly avoided the regional newsstand that featured stories about domestic violence. The tight feedback loop of avoidance, hyper-vigilance, and sensory recall had narrowed his world to a single, exhausting purpose: surviving the next moment. It was this mounting isolation and the fear that his own nervous system would betray him at any second that finally brought Arthur to seek help, hoping not to erase the past, but to reclaim the ability to walk through a room without bracing for a blow that was long over.
